# Inferlo: full documentation

Generated from README.md and docs/. Source: https://github.com/BrowserlessAPI/Inferlo

---

# Inferlo

**The enterprise-ready TypeScript backend framework, with AI models built in.**

Inferlo is a batteries-included TypeScript backend framework for production APIs, SaaS products and enterprise services, in the same class as NestJS, Fastify and AdonisJS. It gives you routing, validation, a typed database layer with PostgreSQL and migrations, auth, rate limiting, background jobs, cron, OpenAPI and secure defaults in one package with zero runtime dependencies, running on Node.js, Bun and edge runtimes.

What sets it apart is that AI models are part of the core, not a plugin: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, local models through Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible server behind one API, with fallback between models, typed structured output, streaming, tool calling, image input and per-user usage and cost tracking, plus an MCP server built from your routes.

```ts
import { model, route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const Ticket = model("tickets", {
  title: t.string().min(3).max(200),
  body: t.text(),
  priority: t.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]).default("normal"),
  ownerId: t.ref("users"),
});

export const createTicket = route
  .post("/tickets", { body: Ticket.pick("title", "body"), tool: true })
  .handle(({ body, user, db }) => db.tickets.insert({ ...body, ownerId: user.id }));

export const triageTicket = route
  .post("/tickets/:id/triage", { params: t.object({ id: t.uuid() }), auth: "agent" })
  .handle(async ({ params, db, ai, user }) => {
    const ticket = await db.tickets.get(params.id);
    const { object } = await ai.generate({
      model: "fast",
      prompt: ticket.body,
      output: t.object({ priority: Ticket.fields.priority, summary: t.string().max(300) }),
      for: user.id,
    });
    return db.tickets.update(ticket.id, object);
  });
```

That one model definition gives you the database table, insert and update validation, TypeScript types, OpenAPI docs, an MCP tool and the AI output schema.

## AI models built in

- **Every major provider, one API.** Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible server (DeepSeek, Qwen, Groq, OpenRouter, vLLM and more).
- **Model aliases with fallback.** Routes ask for `"fast"` or `"smart"`; if the first model is down or rate limited, Inferlo tries the next one.
- **Typed structured output.** Pass a schema and get validated, typed data back. Invalid answers are repaired automatically.
- **Tool calling.** Pass routes as `tools` and the model calls them as the current user, with the same auth and validation, or plain functions made with `tool(name, { description, input }).handle(fn)`, with validated arguments; a step limit and usage per step either way.
- **Streaming.** Send model output to the browser as it is generated with one call.
- **Images.** Send image URLs or base64 data with a prompt to any vision model.
- **Embeddings** for search and recommendations.
- **Usage, cost and budgets.** Every call is tracked per user, so you can bill customers and stop calls when their credits run out.
- **MCP server.** Mark a route `tool: true` and AI agents can call your API, with the same permissions as any other client.
- **Use it in any framework.** `import { createAI } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai"` gives you the same AI module without `createApp`, for Express, Hono, Fastify, NestJS or a plain script, and `toNodeHandler(app, { prefix: "/ai" })` mounts a whole Inferlo app (routes, OpenAPI, MCP) inside Express, Fastify, NestJS or `node:http`, `hono.use(inferloAI(ai))` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/hono` gives Hono handlers `c.var.ai`, `server.use(inferloAI(ai))` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/express` gives Express handlers `req.ai`, and `fastify.register(inferloPlugin, { ai })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/fastify` gives Fastify `request.ai`, `new Elysia().use(inferloAI(ai))` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/elysia` gives Elysia handlers `ai`, `InferloModule.forRoot({ ai })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/nestjs` makes the AI client injectable in NestJS, the provider from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/adonisjs` gives AdonisJS routes `ctx.ai`, `@Configuration({ imports: [inferloAI(ai)] })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/tsed` makes the AI client injectable in Ts.ED as `InferloAI`, `trpc.procedure.use(inferloAI(ai))` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/trpc` gives tRPC procedures `ctx.ai` while `trpcTools(router, { caller, procedures })` lets a model call tRPC procedures as tools, `koa.use(inferloAI(ai))` and `koa.use(toKoaMiddleware(app, { prefix: "/api" }))` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/koa` give Koa `ctx.ai` and a whole Inferlo app, `export const { GET, POST } = toNextHandlers(app, { prefix: "/api" })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/nextjs` serves a whole Inferlo app from a Next.js App Router route, `export default toH3Handler(app, { prefix: "/api" })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/h3` serves it from a Nuxt or Nitro server route (with `event.context.ai` from a Nitro plugin), `export const { GET, POST, fallback } = toSvelteKitHandlers(app, { prefix: "/api" })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/sveltekit` serves it from a SvelteKit rest route (with `event.locals.ai` from a handle hook), `export const { loader, action } = toReactRouterHandlers(app, { prefix: "/api" })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/react-router` serves it from a React Router (Remix) resource route, and an Encore.ts raw endpoint serves a whole Inferlo app with `api.raw({ expose: true, method: "*", path: "/inferlo/*rest" }, toNodeHandler(app, { prefix: "/inferlo" }))` (see [Use with other frameworks](docs/integrations.md)).
- **Background jobs for slow AI work.** Queue a typed job from a route with `ctx.jobs.enqueue(...)` and it runs after the response, with retries, from a Postgres queue shared by every instance (`inferlo worker` runs them in their own process), and schedule jobs with `cron("0 3 * * *", job)`.

## Why Inferlo

See the full [comparison with NestJS, AdonisJS, Fastify, Hono, ElysiaJS, Ts.ED, tRPC and Encore.ts](docs/comparison.md). Inferlo's AI features work inside each of those frameworks, and a whole Inferlo app mounts inside them (see [Use with other frameworks](docs/integrations.md)).

| | NestJS | Hono | AdonisJS | Express | **Inferlo** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batteries included (DB, validation, auth) | Partial | No | Yes | No | **Yes** |
| Runs on Node, Bun, Deno and edge | No | Yes | No | No | **Yes** |
| One schema for DB, validation, API docs and AI | No | No | No | No | **Yes** |
| AI providers, fallback, structured output, streaming in core | No | No | No | No | **Yes** |
| Built-in MCP server from your routes | No | No | No | No | **Yes** |
| Token usage tracking and budgets | No | No | No | No | **Yes** |
| Private routes by default | No | No | No | No | **Yes** |
| Errors with codes, fixes and docs links | No | No | Partial | No | **Yes** |
| Zero runtime dependencies | No | Yes | No | No | **Yes** |

## Easy to build with AI coding tools

Inferlo is also designed so AI coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, NeonCodex and others) write correct Inferlo code on the first try:

- **Familiar shapes.** Hono-style routes and Zod-style schemas: patterns models already know.
- **One way to do things.** One route API, one schema API, one query API, one AI API.
- **No hidden behaviour.** No decorators, no dependency injection, no global registration. Everything a handler needs is in its file.
- **Types catch invented code.** Misspelled fields, missing tables and wrong types fail at compile time. At runtime, unknown fields are rejected with "Did you mean ...?".
- **Errors that explain the fix.** Every error has a stable code (`IL1001`), the cause, the fix and a docs link.
- **Tools for agents.** `inferlo describe --json` returns the whole app map. `inferlo check --json` returns typecheck, load and test results as JSON. `inferlo add resource` generates correct CRUD code.
- **Docs for machines.** [`llms.txt`](llms.txt), [`llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt), and every new project ships with `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.
- **Secure by default.** Routes require a signed-in user unless marked public, every query is parameterised, and every insert is validated, so AI-written code stays safe even with light review.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.18+ or Bun 1.3+. TypeScript runs directly with no build step.

Every release is tested on Node.js 22.18, 22, 24, 26 and the current release; Bun 1.3.0 and latest; PostgreSQL 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and latest; and TypeScript 5.9 and latest.

```bash
npx @browserlessapi/inferlo new my-app
cd my-app && npm install && npm run dev
```

Or add it to an existing project:

```bash
npm install @browserlessapi/inferlo
```

## Features

- **Routing:** `route.get/post/put/patch/delete`, typed path params, query coercion, CORS, middleware, body limits
- **Schemas:** `t.string()`, `t.email()`, `t.enum()`, `t.ref()`, ... with `.optional()`, `.default()`, `.pick()`, `.partial()`, JSON Schema output
- **Database:** typed tables (`db.tickets.findMany(...)`), PostgreSQL and in-memory adapters, `inferlo db push`, versioned migrations (`inferlo db migrate`), transactions, unique and foreign keys
- **Auth:** `auth.resolve(req)`, `bearer()` API keys, roles, password hashing with Web Crypto
- **AI:** Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible server; aliases with fallback; structured output with automatic repair; streaming to SSE; embeddings; per-user usage and cost tracking; budgets
- **MCP:** routes with `tool: true` become MCP tools at `/mcp`, with the same auth as HTTP
- **OpenAPI 3.1** at `/openapi.json`
- **Testing:** `app.request(path, { json, as: user })`, `mockProvider()`, `memory()`
- **CLI:** `new`, `dev`, `describe`, `check`, `db push`, `db migrate`, `openapi`, `add resource`

# Getting started

Inferlo needs Node.js 22.18 or newer (or Bun 1.3+). TypeScript runs directly, with no build step.

## Create a project

```bash
npx @browserlessapi/inferlo new my-app
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
```

`npm run dev` starts the server on http://localhost:3000 with an in-memory database and prints a dev API key:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/notes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dev_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Hello"}'
```

## Project layout

```
src/
  config.ts        settings: every environment variable, validated at startup
  models.ts        every model and the models array
  routes/notes.ts  routes for one feature
  app.ts           createApp({ models, routes, db, auth, ai })
  server.ts        starts the HTTP server
test/notes.test.ts
AGENTS.md          rules for AI coding agents
```

## The whole framework in one file

```ts
import { createApp, model, route, t, bearer } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const User = model("users", {
  email: t.email().unique(),
  name: t.string().max(80),
});

export const Todo = model("todos", {
  title: t.string().min(1).max(200),
  done: t.boolean().default(false),
  ownerId: t.ref("users"),
});

export const models = [User, Todo] as const;

// Register once so ctx.db and ctx.user are typed in every handler.
declare module "@browserlessapi/inferlo" {
  interface Register {
    models: typeof models;
    user: { id: string };
  }
}

export const listTodos = route
  .get("/todos", { query: t.object({ done: t.boolean().optional() }) })
  .handle(({ query, user, db }) => db.todos.findMany({ where: { ownerId: user.id, done: query.done } }));

export const createTodo = route
  .post("/todos", { body: Todo.pick("title") })
  .handle(({ body, user, db }) => db.todos.insert({ ...body, ownerId: user.id }));

export const app = createApp({
  models,
  routes: [{ listTodos, createTodo }],
  // Look up the user for the token. See docs/auth.md for API keys stored as hashes.
  auth: bearer(async (token) => (token === process.env.DEMO_TOKEN ? { id: "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001" } : null)),
});
```

# Inferlo compared with other TypeScript backend frameworks

| Framework | Primary focus | Best for | Structural style |
|---|---|---|---|
| NestJS | Architecture and modules | Enterprise apps and large teams | Heavy (decorators, dependency injection) |
| AdonisJS | Full-stack productivity | Rapid MVPs and monoliths | Batteries-included MVC |
| Fastify | Speed and validation | High-throughput JSON APIs | Plugin-based |
| Hono | Edge and web standards | Serverless and edge runtimes | Minimal, Express-like |
| ElysiaJS | Bun performance and end-to-end types | Fast APIs on Bun | Chained, type-inferred |
| Ts.ED | Structured Express/Koa apps | Teams that like classes and decorators | Decorators on Express or Koa |
| tRPC | End-to-end type safety | Full-stack TypeScript monorepos | Schema-driven RPC |
| Encore.ts | Infrastructure from code | Microservices on AWS and GCP | Declarative SDK |
| **Inferlo** | **Enterprise backends with AI models built in** | **Production APIs, SaaS and enterprise services, especially ones with AI features (chat, agents, tool calling, AI billed per user)** | **Batteries-included and modular, plain functions (no decorators)** |

## What Inferlo offers

- **A complete backend framework:** routes, validation, typed database layer with PostgreSQL and migrations, auth, rate limiting, background jobs and cron, OpenAPI, secure defaults (routes private unless marked public, parameterised queries, validated input), stable error codes, tested on the oldest supported and latest Node.js, Bun, PostgreSQL and TypeScript versions.

- **AI models in the core:** Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible server behind one API, with fallback between models, typed structured output, streaming, embeddings, image input and per-user usage and cost tracking.
- **Tool calling with your own routes:** a model can call your routes as tools, with the same permissions as the signed-in user.
- **MCP server:** mark a route `tool: true` and AI agents such as Claude Code or Cursor can call your API.
- **One schema** for the database table, validation, TypeScript types, OpenAPI and AI output.
- **Batteries included:** routes, PostgreSQL, migrations, auth, rate limiting, background jobs and cron.
- **Structure for large codebases:** feature modules (`module("billing", { imports, models, routes, jobs, provides })`) with explicit, checked dependencies and no dependency injection container.
- **Runs on Node.js, Bun and edge runtimes,** with zero runtime dependencies.

## Choose Inferlo when

- you want one batteries-included framework for production APIs and services, with secure defaults and no decorators;
- your API calls AI models (chat, summarising, extraction, agents) and you want providers, fallback, streaming and cost tracking handled for you;
- you want AI agents to use your API through MCP or tool calling, with your existing permissions;
- you want everything (database, auth, jobs, AI) set up out of the box, without decorators.

Choose another framework when you need its specific strength, for example NestJS for a large team that already uses its module system, or Encore.ts to provision cloud infrastructure from code. Inferlo is a young project (version 0.x); check the [changelog](../CHANGELOG.md) and [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md).

## Using Inferlo with another framework

Planned (see the roadmap): use Inferlo's AI module on its own inside any of these frameworks, or mount a whole Inferlo app inside them, with a tested example for each one.

---

# Configuration

`config({ schema })` reads every environment variable your app uses, validates them once at startup and gives you typed values. A missing or invalid variable stops the app with one error that lists every problem, instead of failing later in a request.

```ts
// src/config.ts
import { config, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const settings = config({
  schema: t.object({
    DATABASE_URL: t.string(),
    PORT: t.int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),
    LOG_LEVEL: t.enum(["debug", "info", "warn", "error"]).default("info"),
    DEBUG: t.boolean().default(false),
    ALLOWED_ORIGINS: t.array(t.string()).default(() => []),   // "https://a.io,https://b.io"
    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: t.string().min(10),
    SENTRY_DSN: t.string().optional(),
  }),
  secrets: ["DATABASE_URL", "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"],
  environments: {
    test: { DATABASE_URL: "postgres://localhost/app_test", ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: "sk-test-not-used", LOG_LEVEL: "warn" },
  },
});

settings.PORT;      // number
settings.LOG_LEVEL; // "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error"
```

Use `settings` everywhere instead of reading `process.env` or calling `env()` in routes, so every variable the app needs is in one file.

## Where values come from

For each field, in this order:

1. The environment variable with the field's name. Empty values count as not set. `inferlo dev` and `inferlo worker` read `.env` into the environment first (variables that are already set win), and Bun reads `.env` files itself.
2. `environments[<current environment>]`, for example fixed values for tests.
3. The field's `.default(...)`. Fields without a default must be set, unless they are `.optional()`.

The current environment is `options.environment`, else `INFERLO_ENV`, else `NODE_ENV`, else `"development"`.

Values are converted to the field's type: numbers for `t.int()` and `t.number()`, `true` for `1`, `true`, `yes` and `on` and `false` for `0`, `false`, `no` and `off` with `t.boolean()`, and comma-separated lists for `t.array(...)`. All other `t.*` rules apply (`.min`, `.max`, `.regex`, `t.enum`, `t.email`, `t.url`, `t.uuid`). Fields must not be objects (environment variables are text); use `t.json()` and parse it yourself if you need that.

## Errors

A missing or invalid value throws IL7003 at startup:

```
IL7003  Configuration is invalid (environment "production"). DATABASE_URL: Required. PORT: Expected a number, got string. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: Invalid value (secret, not shown).
```

`error.details` is `{ environment, issues: [{ key, code, message }] }`. Mistakes in the options themselves (a secret or an `environments` key that is not in the schema, a schema that is not `t.object`) throw IL7004.

## Secrets

Fields listed in `secrets` are never shown: `JSON.stringify(settings)`, `console.log(settings)` and `String(settings)` print `"[redacted]"` instead of their values, and IL7003 does not include them. Reading `settings.DATABASE_URL` in code still gives the real value, so pass it to `postgres({ url })` or a provider, never to a log line. List every API key, password, token and connection URL as a secret.

Pass the settings to `createApp({ redact: [settings] })` (new projects do) and the values of its secrets are also replaced with `"[redacted]"` wherever they turn up in what the app logs, for example inside an error message from another service. See [secrets in logs](security.md#secrets-in-logs).

The returned object is frozen, so code cannot change configuration at runtime.

## Testing

In a test, `setEnv({ PORT: "0", DATABASE_URL: undefined })` overrides variables for `config()` and `env()` (names you leave out are still read from the environment), and `setEnv(undefined)` removes the overrides. Or set `NODE_ENV=test` (Bun's test runner does) and keep test values in `environments.test`.

---

# Schemas

`t` builds schemas. One schema gives you runtime validation, a TypeScript type, JSON Schema (for OpenAPI, MCP tools and AI structured output) and a database column.

```ts
import { t, type Infer } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

const Signup = t.object({
  email: t.email(),
  name: t.string().min(1).max(80),
  plan: t.enum(["free", "pro"]).default("free"),
  referral: t.string().optional(),
});

type Signup = Infer<typeof Signup>;
// { email: string; name: string; plan: "free" | "pro"; referral?: string }
```

## Types

| Builder | TypeScript | Postgres column |
|---|---|---|
| `t.string()` | `string` | `text`, or `varchar(n)` with `.max(n)` |
| `t.text()` | `string` | `text` |
| `t.email()` | `string` | `text` |
| `t.url()` | `string` (http/https only) | `text` |
| `t.uuid()` | `string` | `uuid` |
| `t.ref("users")` | `string` (id of a row) | `uuid` + foreign key + index |
| `t.int()` | `number` (whole) | `integer` |
| `t.number()` | `number` | `double precision` |
| `t.boolean()` | `boolean` | `boolean` |
| `t.date()` | `Date` (accepts ISO strings) | `timestamptz` |
| `t.enum(["a", "b"])` | `"a" \| "b"` | `text` + check constraint |
| `t.literal("x")` | `"x"` | `text` |
| `t.array(t.string())` | `string[]` | `jsonb` |
| `t.object({...})` | object | `jsonb` |
| `t.json<T>()` | `T` | `jsonb` |
| `t.any()` | `unknown` | `jsonb` |

## Modifiers

| Modifier | Effect |
|---|---|
| `.optional()` | May be left out |
| `.nullable()` | May be `null` |
| `.default(value)` | Used when left out. Pass a function for fresh values: `.default(() => [])` |
| `.min(n)` / `.max(n)` | Length for strings and arrays, value for numbers |
| `.regex(/.../)` | Strings must match |
| `.describe("...")` | Shown in OpenAPI, MCP tools and AI prompts |
| `.unique()` / `.index()` | Database unique index / index |

Object schemas also have `.pick(...)`, `.omit(...)`, `.partial()`, `.extend({...})` and `.strip()`.

## Unknown keys are rejected

Objects reject fields that are not in the schema, with a hint:

```
Unknown field "titel". Did you mean "title"?
```

This catches typos and invented fields early. Call `.strip()` to drop unknown keys silently instead. Query strings always ignore unknown keys.

## Validating

```ts
Signup.parse(input);        // returns typed data or throws ValidationError (IL1001, HTTP 422)
Signup.safeParse(input);    // { ok: true, value } or { ok: false, issues }
Signup.toJSONSchema();      // JSON Schema object
```

Pass `{ coerce: true }` to convert strings to numbers, booleans and arrays (Inferlo does this automatically for query strings and path parameters).

---

# Models and database

## Models

```ts
import { model, t, type Row } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const Ticket = model("tickets", {
  title: t.string().min(3).max(200),
  priority: t.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]).default("normal"),
  status: t.enum(["open", "closed"]).default("open").index(),
  ownerId: t.ref("users", { onDelete: "cascade" }),
});

type Ticket = Row<typeof Ticket>;
```

- The first argument is the table name and the property on `db` (`db.tickets`). Lowercase with underscores.
- Every model gets `id` (uuid), `createdAt` and `updatedAt`. Do not define them.
- Fields are camelCase in code and snake_case in the database (`ownerId` is `owner_id`).
- `Ticket.create` is the insert schema, `Ticket.update` the update schema, `Ticket.pick(...)` / `Ticket.omit(...)` give route body schemas.

## Register your models once

```ts
// src/models.ts
export const models = [User, Ticket] as const;

declare module "@browserlessapi/inferlo" {
  interface Register {
    models: typeof models;
    user: AppUser;
  }
}
```

After this, `ctx.db` in every handler is fully typed.

## Queries

```ts
await db.tickets.insert({ title: "Down", ownerId: user.id });          // validated, returns the row
await db.tickets.find(id);                                              // row or null
await db.tickets.get(id);                                               // row, or throws IL4001 (404)
await db.tickets.findOne({ ownerId: user.id, status: "open" });
await db.tickets.findMany({
  where: { status: "open", priority: { in: ["normal", "urgent"] }, createdAt: { gte: since } },
  orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
  limit: 20,      // default 100, max 1000
  offset: 0,
});
await db.tickets.count({ status: "open" });
await db.tickets.paginate({ where: { status: "open" }, orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }, cursor, limit: 20 }); // { items, nextCursor }, see Pagination
await db.tickets.update(id, { status: "closed" });                      // validated, throws 404 if missing
await db.tickets.updateMany({ ownerId: user.id }, { status: "closed" });
await db.tickets.delete(id);                                            // true if deleted
await db.tickets.deleteMany({ status: "closed" });                      // a filter is required
```

Where operators: `eq`, `ne`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `in`, `notIn`, `like`, `ilike`, `isNull`. A plain value means `eq`; `null` means `isNull: true`; `undefined` is ignored, so optional filters can be passed directly.

Unknown fields or operators raise IL4003 with a "Did you mean" hint.

## Relations

Every `t.ref` field named `<name>Id` is a relation called `<name>`: `ownerId: t.ref("users")` gives `owner`. Load related rows with `include`:

```ts
const tickets = await db.tickets.findMany({ where: { status: "open" }, include: { owner: true } });
tickets[0].owner.name;    // Row<typeof User>, fully typed

const ticket = await db.tickets.get(id, { include: { owner: true, assignee: true } });
ticket.assignee?.name;    // optional or nullable refs give Row | null
```

- `include` works on `findMany`, `findOne(where, { include })`, `find(id, { include })` and `get(id, { include })`.
- Each relation costs **one extra query** for all rows together (`WHERE id IN (...)`), never one query per row.
- Rows keep the id field (`ownerId`) and get the related row under the relation name (`owner`). A missing related row is `null`.
- Ref fields whose name does not end in `Id`, or whose relation name is already a field, are not relations. Unknown names raise IL4023, listing the relations the model has.

### Reverse (has-many) relations

The other direction works too: include the rows that point to this one by their **table name**. If `tickets` has `ownerId: t.ref("users")`, then:

```ts
const users = await db.users.findMany({ include: { tickets: true } });
users[0].tickets;         // Row<typeof Ticket>[], [] when there are none

const team = await db.teams.get(id, { include: { tickets: true } });
```

- One extra query per relation for all rows together (`WHERE owner_id IN (...)`), ordered by `createdAt`, then `id`.
- Every related row is loaded. For large lists, query the other table with `findMany({ where: { ownerId: user.id }, limit })` instead.
- If the other table has **several** ref fields to this model (`ownerId` and `assigneeId`), each is named `<table>By<Name>`: `include: { ticketsByOwner: true, ticketsByAssignee: true }`. The plain table name is then ambiguous and raises IL4023, naming both.
- A reverse name that is already a field or a relation of this model is not available.
- Forward and reverse relations can be combined in one `include`.

## Pagination

`paginate` returns one page and a cursor for the next one. Pass `nextCursor` back as `cursor`; it is `null` on the last page.

```ts
export const listTickets = route
  .get("/tickets", { query: t.object({ limit: t.int().min(1).max(100).default(20), cursor: t.string().max(500).optional() }) })
  .handle(({ query, user, db }) =>
    db.tickets.paginate({ where: { ownerId: user.id }, orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }, limit: query.limit, cursor: query.cursor }),
  );
// { "items": [...], "nextCursor": "eyJmIjoiY3JlYXRlZEF0Ii..." }
```

- **Stable pages.** Pagination is by key (the last row's value and id), not by offset, so pages never skip or repeat rows when rows are added or deleted elsewhere in the list, and deep pages are as fast as the first.
- **Order** by one field: `orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }` (the default is `{ createdAt: "asc" }`). Rows with the same value are ordered by `id`. The field must be required (not `.optional()` without a default, not `.nullable()`) and not `json`, `array` or `object`; otherwise IL4025. More than one field, or `offset`, also raises IL4025.
- `where`, `limit` (default 100, maximum 1000) and `include` work as in `findMany`. A page costs one query, or two after the first page when ordering by a field other than `id`, plus one per included relation.
- **Cursors** are opaque strings. Pass them back unchanged with the same `orderBy`. A cursor that was changed, is not from `paginate`, or was made for another order raises IL4024 with status 400, so a bad `?cursor=` from a client is a 400 response. Cursors are not secret: they contain the last row's id and order value, and `where` still applies to every page.
- For numbered pages ("page 3 of 12"), use `findMany({ limit, offset })` with `count(where)`.

## Adapters

```ts
import { memory } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { postgres } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/postgres";

createApp({ db: memory() });                                  // tests and prototypes
createApp({ db: postgres({ url: env("DATABASE_URL") }) });    // production (npm install pg)
```

## Schema changes

```bash
inferlo db push --dry-run   # show the SQL
inferlo db push             # create missing tables, columns and indexes
```

`db push` only adds things; it never drops or renames columns. New columns on existing tables should be `.optional()` or have a `.default()`. Use it for development and prototypes; use migrations in production.

## Migrations

```bash
inferlo db migrate add_due_dates   # write migrations/0002_add_due_dates.sql for your model changes
inferlo db migrate --dry-run       # print the SQL without writing anything
inferlo db migrate drop_color --allow-drop   # include drops of tables, columns and indexes (deletes data)
inferlo db migrate require_body --allow-change   # include type, default, required/optional and enum value changes
inferlo db migrate --apply         # run pending migration files against DATABASE_URL
```

- `inferlo db migrate [name]` compares your models with `migrations/snapshot.json` (your models as of the last generated migration), writes the SQL for the difference to the next numbered file and updates the snapshot. With no changes it writes nothing. Commit both files.
- Review the generated SQL before applying it. You may edit a file until it has been applied anywhere; after that, add a new migration instead.
- `--apply` runs every file not yet recorded in the `inferlo_migrations` table, in file name order, each in its own transaction, and records it with a SHA-256 checksum of its SQL. It is safe to run on every deploy and from several instances at once. Do not put `BEGIN` or `COMMIT` in migration files.
- If a file that was already applied has been edited since, `--apply` does not run it again: it prints warning IL4018 naming the file (and lists it in `edited` with `--json`), and still applies the pending files. Restore the applied SQL (for example with `git checkout`) and put the change in a new migration. Line ending changes (CRLF and LF) do not count as edits. Migrations applied with Inferlo 0.2 get their checksum recorded from the current file on the next `--apply`.
- Generated statements use `IF NOT EXISTS`, so the first migration also works on a database created with `db push`.
- New tables, columns and indexes are generated directly. A new required column on an existing table raises IL4014: give it a fixed `.default(value)` or make it `.optional()`.
- Removing a model, field, `.unique()` or `.index()` drops data, so it raises IL4017 and nothing is written, unless you pass `--allow-drop`. Then the file gets `DROP INDEX`, `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` and `DROP TABLE` statements (without `CASCADE`) and a warning comment, and `--json` output lists them in `drops`. Back up before applying it.
- Changing a field's default, making it required or optional, or changing an enum's values raises IL4019 and nothing is written, unless you pass `--allow-change`. Then the file gets `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ...` with `SET DEFAULT`, `DROP DEFAULT`, `SET NOT NULL` or `DROP NOT NULL`, and `--json` output lists the changes in `changes`, for example `change column notes.body (optional -> required, default none -> '')`. A function default (`.default(() => ...)`) is filled in by Inferlo, not the database, so it counts as no default (`DROP DEFAULT`).
- Making a field required: if it has a fixed `.default(value)`, rows that are NULL get that value first (`UPDATE ... WHERE ... IS NULL`), as for a new required column. Without a default, `--apply` fails with IL4020 if any row is still NULL, and nothing from that migration is kept. Add an `UPDATE` that fills them before the `SET NOT NULL` (only in a file that has not been applied anywhere), or give the field a default.
- Changing an enum's values (adding or removing one, or turning a text field into an enum or back) also needs `--allow-change`. The file replaces the column's CHECK constraint: `ALTER TABLE "posts" DROP CONSTRAINT "posts_kind_check"`, then `ALTER TABLE "posts" ADD CONSTRAINT "posts_kind_check" CHECK ("kind" IN ('note', 'page'))`, using the name Postgres gave it. Adding a value always works. If rows still use a removed value, `--apply` fails with IL4021 and nothing from that migration is kept: in a file that has not been applied anywhere, add `UPDATE "posts" SET "kind" = 'page' WHERE "kind" = 'article';` before the `ADD CONSTRAINT`, or keep the value.
- Changing a field's type (for example `t.string().max(120)` to `.max(200)`, `t.text()` to `t.int()`, or `t.int()` to `t.number()`) also needs `--allow-change`. The file gets `ALTER TABLE "posts" ALTER COLUMN "title" TYPE varchar(200)`, with a `USING` clause when Postgres needs one: other types go through their text (`USING "views"::text::integer`), jsonb values use their JSON text (`USING ("meta" #>> '{}')::integer`), and a field becoming `t.json()` uses `to_jsonb(...)`, so text becomes a JSON string. A fixed default is dropped before the type change and set again after it. Conversions are strict: a value that does not fit (text that is not a number, `2.5` going to `integer`, text longer than the new `varchar(n)`) is never cut, rounded or set to NULL; `--apply` fails with IL4022 and nothing from that migration is kept. In a file that has not been applied anywhere, add an `UPDATE` before the `TYPE` statement that fixes those values, or write your own `USING` expression.
- Renames and reference changes are not generated yet: they raise IL4013 and nothing is written. The message says what changed in each column, for example `change column posts.author_id (reference authors on delete cascade -> authors on delete restrict)`, and `details.columns` lists the same as `{ table, column, changes }`. A rename looks like a drop plus an add; do not use `--allow-drop` for a rename, or the column's data is lost.
- `snapshot.json` describes each column as `{ type, notNull, default?, enum?, references?, primaryKey? }` (format `"inferlo": 2`). Snapshots written by Inferlo 0.2.0 (`"inferlo": 1`, each column as SQL text) are read as they are and saved in the new format with the next generated migration. Do not edit the snapshot by hand; an invalid one raises IL4015.

To apply migrations from code, for example at startup in a serverless function:

```ts
import { applyMigrations } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

await applyMigrations(app.db, [{ name: "0001_init", sql: initSql }]);   // returns the names it applied

// Applied migrations whose SQL changed since are not run again; onEdited gets their names (IL4018).
await applyMigrations(app.db, migrations, { onEdited: (names) => console.warn("Edited after apply:", names) });
```

To generate SQL from code, use `planMigration(models, snapshot, { allowDrop, allowChange })`. It returns `{ statements, snapshot, drops, changes }`:

```ts
import { planMigration } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

const plan = planMigration(models, previousSnapshot, { allowDrop: true });   // allowDrop and allowChange default to false
```

## Transactions and raw SQL (Postgres)

```ts
await db.$transaction(async (tx) => {
  const order = await tx.orders.insert({ ... });
  await tx.order_items.insertMany(items.map((i) => ({ ...i, orderId: order.id })));
});

await db.$sql("select count(*) from tickets where owner_id = $1", [user.id]);   // always use $1 placeholders
```

---

# Routes

```ts
import { route, t, notFound } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const getTicket = route
  .get("/tickets/:id", {
    params: t.object({ id: t.uuid() }),
    summary: "Get one ticket",
    tool: true,
  })
  .handle(async ({ params, user, db }) => {
    const ticket = await db.tickets.get(params.id);
    if (ticket.ownerId !== user.id) throw notFound();
    return ticket;
  });
```

Methods: `route.get`, `route.post`, `route.put`, `route.patch`, `route.delete`. HEAD is answered by GET routes.

## Options

| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `auth` | `"user"` (default, signed in), `"public"`, or a role name such as `"admin"` |
| `body` | Request body schema (JSON or form-encoded) |
| `query` | Query string schema. Values are converted to numbers and booleans; unknown keys ignored |
| `params` | Path parameter schema. Without it, params are strings |
| `response` | Response schema for OpenAPI |
| `summary`, `description`, `tags` | Documentation for OpenAPI, describe and MCP |
| `tool` | `true` or `{ name, description }` to expose the route as an MCP tool |
| `rateLimit` | `{ max, per, by }` to limit requests per user or IP (see below) |
| `deprecated` | `true`, or `{ since, sunset, link }` to send deprecation headers (see below) |
| `cache` | `{ ttlMs, by: "user" \| "public", tags }` to cache a GET route's JSON responses (see [Caching](caching.md#caching-route-responses)) |
| `timeoutMs` | Time limit in milliseconds for this route, or `false` for none. Default: `createApp({ requestTimeoutMs })`, 60000. Slower requests answer 503 IL2007 (see [request timeouts](security.md#request-timeouts)) |

Paths support `:param` segments and a final `*` wildcard (`params["*"]`).

## Rate limiting

```ts
export const login = route
  .post("/login", { auth: "public", body: Login, rateLimit: { max: 5, per: "minute", by: "ip" } })
  .handle(...);

export const summarize = route
  .post("/notes/:id/summary", { params: IdParams, rateLimit: { max: 20, per: "hour" } })   // by: "user" is the default
  .handle(...);
```

- `max` requests per `per` (`"second"`, `"minute"`, `"hour"` or `"day"`), in fixed windows, counted separately for each route.
- `by: "user"` (default) counts each signed-in user; requests without a user (on public routes) count by IP. `by: "ip"` counts each client IP.
- The count is checked after auth and before input validation: failed sign-ins on private routes do not use it up, invalid bodies do.
- Over the limit the route answers **429** with IL2005 and a `Retry-After` header. Every response of a limited route has `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` (seconds) headers.
- Tool calls from `ai.generate({ tools })` and the MCP server count too, as the same user.
- Counts are kept in memory by default (one process, tests). With several instances, keep them in Postgres: `createApp({ rateLimit: { store: "database" } })` uses the `inferlo_rate_limits` table, created on first use (IL6008 without Postgres).
- The client IP comes from the server (`app.listen()`, Bun and Deno). Behind a load balancer or proxy, set `createApp({ trustProxy: true })` to use the first `X-Forwarded-For` address; leave it off otherwise, because clients can send that header themselves.
- Invalid options raise IL6007 when the app starts.

## Deprecating routes

When a route is replaced (for example `/v1/tickets` by `/v2/tickets`, see [API versions](#api-versions)), mark the old one deprecated instead of removing it at once, so clients have time to move:

```ts
export const listTicketsV1 = route
  .get("/v1/tickets", {
    deprecated: { since: "2026-11-01", sunset: "2027-06-30", link: "https://example.com/docs/tickets-v2" },
  })
  .handle(...);
```

- Every response of the route, errors included, gets the standard headers that HTTP clients, API gateways and SDK generators read: `Deprecation: @1793491200` ([RFC 9745](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745), the `since` date as Unix seconds), `Sunset: Wed, 30 Jun 2027 00:00:00 GMT` ([RFC 8594](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594)) and `Link: <https://example.com/docs/tickets-v2>; rel="deprecation"; type="text/html"`. Each header is sent only when its option is set.
- `since` and `sunset` are dates (`"2026-11-01"`), ISO timestamps or `Date` values, and `sunset` must be after `since`. `link` is an http or https URL of a page that explains what to use instead.
- `deprecated: true` marks the route deprecated in OpenAPI, describe and MCP without sending headers.
- OpenAPI marks the operation `deprecated: true` (with the dates and link in `x-inferlo-deprecation`), `describe()` and `inferlo describe` show it, and MCP tool descriptions end with "(Deprecated, stops working on 2027-06-30.)" so AI agents prefer other tools.
- The route keeps working after the sunset date; remove it when you are ready.
- Invalid options raise IL6021 when the app starts, naming the route.

## API versions

When a change would break clients, publish a new API version next to the old one with `apiVersion(version, routes)`:

```ts
import { apiVersion, createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import * as ticketsV1 from "./routes/v1/tickets.ts"; // the old list response
import * as tickets from "./routes/tickets.ts";       // current routes
import * as account from "./routes/account.ts";       // the same in every version

export const app = createApp({
  routes: [
    apiVersion("v1", [ticketsV1, account], { deprecated: { since: "2026-11-01", sunset: "2027-06-30", link: "https://example.com/docs/v2" } }),
    apiVersion("v2", [tickets, account]),
    [auth],                                           // outside every version: /login
  ],
});
```

- Routes are written without the prefix (`route.get("/tickets")`) and served under it: `GET /v1/tickets` and `GET /v2/tickets`. Versions are `"v"` and a number (`"v1"`, `"v2"`).
- A route that did not change goes in several versions (`account` above). Each version gets its own copy under its prefix, so clients of every version reach it at their own base URL.
- Routes in a version are named `<version>_<export name>` (`v1_listTickets`), so OpenAPI operation ids and MCP tool names stay unique.
- `deprecated` on the version marks every route in it, with the Deprecation, Sunset and Link headers described [above](#deprecating-routes). A route's own `deprecated` option wins.
- Each version gets its own OpenAPI document at `/<version>/openapi.json` (`/v1/openapi.json`, following `createApp({ openapi })`), with its routes and the routes outside every version; `app.openapi({ version: "v1" })` returns it. `/openapi.json` still lists every route. SDK generators and API gateways can then be pointed at one version.
- `describe()` lists the versions with the path of each document and gives each route its `version`. Versions work inside [modules](modules.md) too: `module("tickets", { routes: [apiVersion("v2", [tickets])] })`.
- Invalid arguments, a route already in a version, an unknown version in `app.openapi()` and a `GET` route on a version's document path raise IL6025.

## The handler context

| Property | |
|---|---|
| `body`, `query`, `params` | Validated, typed input |
| `user` | The signed-in user (`null` only on public routes without a session) |
| `db` | Typed tables |
| `ai` | `generate`, `stream`, `embed` |
| `jobs` | `enqueue` background jobs (see [Jobs](jobs.md)) |
| `cache` | `getOrSet`, `get`, `set`, `delete`, `invalidate` (see [Caching](caching.md)) |
| `req`, `url`, `headers` | The raw request |
| `status(code)` | Set the status code |
| `header(name, value)` | Set a response header |
| `state` | Per-request values from middleware |
| `signal` | `AbortSignal` aborted when the request times out or the client disconnects. `ai` calls use it automatically; pass it to `fetch` and other slow work |
| `requestId` | This request's id, also in the `X-Request-Id` response header and in its log entries (see [Observability](observability.md)) |
| `waitUntil(promise)` | Work that continues after the response |

## Return values

- Any value is sent as JSON with status 200 (or the code from `status()`).
- `undefined` sends 204 No Content.
- A `Response` is sent as is (files, redirects, streams, `ai.stream(...).toResponse()`).

## Errors

```ts
import { notFound, forbidden, badRequest, httpError } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

throw notFound("Ticket not found");
throw forbidden();
throw badRequest("Pick a future date");
throw httpError(409, "Already paid", { code: "PAYMENT_DONE" });
```

## Registering routes

Export each route as a `const`, then pass the modules:

```ts
import * as tickets from "./routes/tickets.ts";
import * as users from "./routes/users.ts";

createApp({ routes: [tickets, users] });
```

The export name (`getTicket`) becomes the route name used by MCP tools, OpenAPI `operationId` and `inferlo describe`.

## Middleware

```ts
createApp({
  middleware: [
    async ({ req, state }, next) => {
      const started = Date.now();
      const res = await next();
      res.headers.set("x-response-time", `${Date.now() - started}ms`);
      return res;
    },
  ],
});
```

## CORS

```ts
createApp({ cors: { origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true } });
```

---

# Auth

Routes are private by default. Inferlo does not force a login system on you: you give `createApp` an `auth.resolve(req)` that returns the user, and Inferlo enforces route access.

```ts
createApp({
  auth: {
    async resolve(req, { db }) {
      // return the user, or null
    },
    roles: (user) => user.roles,   // optional, default user.roles ?? []
  },
});
```

If any route is private and no `auth` is configured, `createApp` throws IL3003 at startup, so a missing auth setup can never silently expose routes.

## Route access

```ts
route.get("/health", { auth: "public" })     // anyone
route.get("/me")                              // any signed-in user (default)
route.delete("/users/:id", { auth: "admin" }) // users whose roles include "admin"
```

## Permissions

Roles answer "who is this user"; permissions answer "may this user do this, to this record". Define every permission once, by name, in one file, and check it the same way in routes, AI tools and jobs:

```ts
// src/permissions.ts
import { permissions, type AppUser, type Row } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import type { Ticket } from "./models.ts";

export const access = permissions({
  "reports.view": { roles: ["admin", "analyst"] },
  "tickets.update": ({ user, ticket }: { user: AppUser; ticket: Row<typeof Ticket> }) =>
    ticket.ownerId === user.id || (user.roles ?? []).includes("admin"),
});
```

- A rule is either `{ roles: [...] }` (the user has one of these roles in `user.roles`) or a function, sync or async, that receives the user and the records it needs and returns `true` or `false`. Anything else a function returns (`undefined`, a string) is a bug and raises IL6026 instead of allowing.
- Deny by default: without a user (`null` or `undefined`) every permission is denied and the rule is not called. An unknown permission name raises IL6026.
- `await access.can("tickets.update", { user, ticket })` returns `true` or `false`.
- `await access.authorize("tickets.update", { user, ticket })` returns when allowed and otherwise throws IL3004 (403), or IL3001 (401) without a user. Throw it from a handler and the client gets the error.
- The input of `can()` and `authorize()` is typed from the rule, so a missing `ticket` is a type error.

Permissions that need only the user can go on the route. Pass the permissions to `createApp` and set `permission`:

```ts
createApp({ routes, auth, permissions: access });

export const reports = route.get("/reports", { permission: "reports.view", tool: true }).handle(...);

export const updateTicket = route.patch("/tickets/:id", { body: Ticket.pick("title").partial() }).handle(async ({ params, body, user, db }) => {
  const ticket = await db.tickets.get(params.id);
  await access.authorize("tickets.update", { user, ticket });  // 403 IL3004 for other users' tickets
  return db.tickets.update(ticket.id, body);
});
```

- `permission` is checked with `{ user }` after sign-in and before rate limits, validation and the handler. It also applies when a model calls the route as a tool (`ai.generate({ tools })` and MCP), because tools run with the caller's user.
- `createApp` checks at startup that every route's permission exists, that `createApp({ permissions })` is set when a route uses one, and that no route combines `permission` with `auth: "public"` (IL6026).
- `describe()` lists the permissions and each route's `permission`, `inferlo describe` shows them, and OpenAPI marks the route with `x-inferlo-permission` and a 403 response.
- MCP `tools/list` leaves out tools whose role (`auth: "admin"`) or `permission` the caller does not have, so AI agents only see what they may use. Tools that only need a signed-in user stay listed for anonymous callers (calling one answers IL3001), and `tools/call` checks every call as before. A rule that throws while listing hides its tool.
- In jobs there is no signed-in user: pass the user's id in the job input, load the user, and call `access.authorize(name, { user, ... })` before doing the work.
- In tests, call `access.can()` directly, or send requests as a user with `app.request(path, { as: user })`.

### Typed permission names

Add the permissions to `Register` next to your models and user, and the route option `permission` only accepts their names, so a typo is a type error instead of a startup error:

```ts
// src/models.ts
import type { access } from "./permissions.ts";

declare module "@browserlessapi/inferlo" {
  interface Register {
    models: typeof models;
    user: AppUser;
    permissions: typeof access;
  }
}

route.get("/reports", { permission: "reports.view" });   // ok
route.get("/reports", { permission: "report.view" });    // type error
route.get("/tickets/:id", { permission: "tickets.update" }); // type error: the rule needs a ticket, call access.authorize in the handler
```

Only names whose rule needs nothing but `{ user }` (roles rules and functions of the user alone) are accepted, because the route passes only `{ user }`. Use `import type` so the models file does not load the permissions at runtime. Without `permissions` in `Register`, `permission` takes any string and `createApp` still checks it at startup. The type is exported as `AppPermission`.

## Audit log

Record who changed what, from routes and jobs. Add the built-in `AuditLog` model to the app (and to `Register`) and run `inferlo db migrate`, which creates the `audit_log` table:

```ts
import { AuditLog } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const models = [User, Ticket, AuditLog] as const;   // in Register too, so ctx.db.audit_log is typed
```

Then write an entry with `audit` after each change you want on record:

```ts
export const updateTicket = route.patch("/tickets/:id", { body: Ticket.pick("title", "status").partial() }).handle(async ({ params, body, user, db, audit }) => {
  const ticket = await db.tickets.get(params.id);
  await access.authorize("tickets.update", { user, ticket });
  const updated = await db.tickets.update(ticket.id, body);
  await audit("tickets.update", { model: "tickets", before: ticket, after: updated });
  return updated;
});
```

Each entry has:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `action` | The name you pass, such as `"tickets.update"` (use your permission names) |
| `userId` | The signed-in user. In jobs there is none: pass `userId` (the user who asked for the work), or leave it out for work the system does on its own (`null`) |
| `model`, `recordId` | The changed record's model and id (`recordId` defaults to `after.id`, then `before.id`) |
| `changes` | The fields that differ between `before` and `after`, as `{ field: { from, to } }`; leave out `before` for creates and `after` for deletes (missing values are `null`). `id`, `createdAt` and `updatedAt` are skipped and dates are ISO strings |
| `data` | Anything else you pass as `data` |
| `source` | Where it was written: `"PATCH /tickets/:id"` or `"job export-tickets"` |
| `requestId` | The request's id, also in its `X-Request-Id` header and log lines |
| `createdAt` | When |

- Secrets never reach the table: changed fields named like `password`, `token`, `secret`, `apiKey`, `*Hash`, `session` or `cookie` are stored as `"[redacted]"` without their values, the same names in `data` are redacted, and values from `createApp({ redact })` and AI provider keys are replaced inside any string.
- Writing is explicit: nothing is recorded unless you call `audit`, so you choose which actions matter. Call it after the change succeeded. It writes with the request's (or job's) `db`, outside any `db.$transaction`; when the entry must be part of a transaction, insert it with the transaction's client: `tx.audit_log.insert({ action, userId: user.id, model: "tickets", recordId, changes: auditChanges(before, after) })`.
- Read it like any table: `db.audit_log.findMany({ where: { model: "tickets", recordId: id }, orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" } })`. Protect routes that show it with a permission such as `"audit.view"`.
- Without `AuditLog` in the models, `audit` raises IL6027, as do an empty action name or an entry that is not an object. `auditChanges(before, after)` is exported to compute the same `changes` yourself.

## Cookie sessions

For browser apps, `sessions()` signs users in with a cookie: signed with HMAC-SHA256, `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax` by default, with no session table and no runtime dependency. Requests that change data must carry a CSRF token, so other sites cannot act for a signed-in browser.

```ts
// src/session.ts
import { sessions } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { settings } from "./config.ts"; // SESSION_SECRET: t.string().min(32), listed in secrets

export const session = sessions({
  secret: settings.SESSION_SECRET,
  async user({ userId }, { db }) {
    const user = await db.users.find(userId);
    return user ? { id: user.id, email: user.email, name: user.name, roles: [user.role] } : null;
  },
});

// src/app.ts
createApp({ auth: session, ... });
```

Sign in and out in routes:

```ts
import { route, t, verifyPassword } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { session } from "../session.ts";

export const login = route
  .post("/login", { auth: "public", body: t.object({ email: t.string(), password: t.string() }), rateLimit: { max: 10, per: "minute", by: "ip" } })
  .handle(async (ctx) => {
    const user = await ctx.db.users.findOne({ email: ctx.body.email });
    if (!user?.passwordHash || !(await verifyPassword(ctx.body.password, user.passwordHash))) {
      return Response.json({ error: { code: "INVALID_LOGIN", message: "Wrong email or password." } }, { status: 401 });
    }
    return session.signIn(ctx, user.id); // { csrfToken }
  });

export const logout = route.post("/logout").handle((ctx) => {
  session.signOut(ctx);
  ctx.status(204);
  return undefined;
});
```

- `session.signIn(ctx, userId)` sets two cookies: `inferlo_session` (the signed session: user id, issue time and expiry; `HttpOnly`) and `inferlo_session_csrf` (the CSRF token, readable by your frontend's JavaScript). It returns `{ csrfToken }`. `session.signOut(ctx)` clears both.
- **CSRF protection.** A POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE request with a session cookie must send the session's token in an `X-CSRF-Token` header (frontends read it from the `inferlo_session_csrf` cookie or the login answer) or, from an HTML form, a hidden `_csrf` field: `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="...">` with the value of `await session.csrfToken(req)`. Otherwise the request is refused with 403 IL3005 before the handler runs, also on public routes. The `_csrf` field is removed from form bodies before validation. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS never change data, so they need no token.
- `user({ userId, issuedAt }, { db })` runs on every request. Return `null` to end a session: for a deleted or disabled user, or to sign a user out everywhere (store a `sessionsValidAfter` time on the user and return `null` when `issuedAt` is older).
- Options: `maxAgeMs` (default 7 days), `cookie: { name, sameSite: "lax" | "strict", secure, domain, path }`. `Secure` is on except for plain `http://localhost` during development. Rotate the secret with `secret: [newSecret, oldSecret]`: new sessions use the first, existing ones stay valid until they expire.
- Cross-origin frontends need `cors: { origin: "https://app.example.com", credentials: true }`; the `X-CSRF-Token` header is allowed in CORS preflights by default.
- Invalid options raise IL6029 at startup. Tampered, expired or foreign cookies are ignored (the request is signed out).

To accept a session cookie or an API key, try the session first:

```ts
const apiKeys = bearer(async (token, { db }) => { /* as below */ });

createApp({
  auth: {
    async resolve(req, ctx) {
      return (await session.resolve(req, ctx)) ?? apiKeys.resolve(req, ctx);
    },
  },
});
```

## API keys with bearer()

```ts
import { bearer, hashToken, createToken } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

createApp({
  auth: bearer(async (token, { db }) => {
    const key = await db.api_keys.findOne({ hash: await hashToken(token) });
    if (!key) return null;
    const user = await db.users.find(key.userId);
    return user && { id: user.id, email: user.email, name: user.name, roles: [user.role] };
  }),
});

// Issuing a key: show the token once, store only the hash.
const token = createToken("live");
await db.api_keys.insert({ userId, hash: await hashToken(token) });
```

`bearer()` reads `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and falls back to an `x-api-key` header.

## Passwords

```ts
import { hashPassword, verifyPassword } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

const stored = await hashPassword(password);      // PBKDF2-SHA256, 210,000 iterations
const ok = await verifyPassword(password, stored);
```

These use Web Crypto, so they run on Node, Bun, Deno and edge runtimes.

## The user type

Declare your user type once (see [database](database.md#register-your-models-once)) and `ctx.user` is typed in every handler.

---

# AI

Inferlo's AI module gives every route one API for every model provider, with aliases, automatic fallback, typed structured output, streaming, embeddings, usage tracking and budgets.

## Configure

```ts
import { createApp, env, anthropic, openai, gemini, ollama, openaiCompatible } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

createApp({
  ai: {
    providers: {
      anthropic: anthropic({ apiKey: env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") }),
      openai: openai({ apiKey: env("OPENAI_API_KEY") }),
      local: ollama(),
      deepseek: openaiCompatible({ name: "deepseek", baseURL: "https://api.deepseek.com/v1", apiKey: env("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY") }),
    },
    // Aliases: routes use "fast" and "smart", never provider model ids.
    // A list is a fallback order: if the first fails with a timeout, 429 or 5xx, the next is tried.
    models: {
      fast: ["anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5", "openai:gpt-5-mini"],
      smart: ["anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", "openai:gpt-5"],
      embed: "openai:text-embedding-3-small",
    },
    // Optional: USD per million tokens, for cost tracking. Inferlo ships no prices because they change.
    pricing: { "anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5": { input: 1, output: 5 } },
    onUsage: (usage) => console.log(usage),
    allow: async ({ for: userId }) => (await credits(userId)) > 0,
  },
});
```

## Use it without createApp

The AI module also works on its own, in any framework (Express, Hono, Fastify, NestJS, Next.js route handlers), a script or a queue worker. Import it from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai`, which never loads the router, database or jobs code:

```ts
import { createAI, anthropic, openai, env, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai";

export const ai = createAI({
  providers: {
    anthropic: anthropic({ apiKey: env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") }),
    openai: openai({ apiKey: env("OPENAI_API_KEY") }),
  },
  models: { fast: ["anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5", "openai:gpt-5-mini"], embed: "openai:text-embedding-3-small" },
  onUsage: (usage) => console.log(usage),
});

const { object } = await ai.generate({
  model: "fast",
  prompt: "Classify: the export button does nothing",
  output: t.object({ label: t.enum(["bug", "feature", "question"]) }),
  for: userId,
});
```

`createAI` takes the same options as `createApp({ ai })`, and `ai` has the same `generate`, `stream`, `embed` and `aliases` as `ctx.ai` in a route handler. The entry point also exports the providers, `mockProvider` for tests, `t` and `toJSONSchema` for structured output, `tool` for [function tools](#tools-let-the-model-call-your-functions), `env`, `InferloError`, `httpError` and the types (`AI`, `AIConfig`, `Usage`, `Message`, `Provider`, `ToolDef`, ...). Tools made from routes need a route handler (IL5009); function tools work anywhere.

`openaiCompatible()` works with any Chat Completions server: OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen (DashScope), Groq, Together, OpenRouter, vLLM, LM Studio and others.

## Generate text

```ts
const { text, usage } = await ai.generate({
  model: "fast",
  system: "You are a support assistant.",
  prompt: "Reply to: my order is late",
  for: user.id,
});
```

## Images (vision)

Pass images with the prompt to any vision model (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and OpenAI-compatible servers such as Ollama with a vision model):

```ts
const { text } = await ai.generate({
  model: "fast",
  prompt: "What is wrong in this screenshot?",
  images: [{ url: "https://example.com/screenshot.png" }],
  for: user.id,
});

// Base64 data, for example from an upload: no data: prefix, plus the media type.
await ai.generate({ prompt: "Read the receipt total", images: [{ base64: data, mediaType: "image/jpeg" }], output: Receipt });
```

- An image is `{ url }` (`https://`, `http://` or a `data:image/...;base64,` URL) or `{ base64, mediaType }`. Media types: `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`.
- In a conversation, put images on user messages: `messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Here is the receipt", images: [...] }]`.
- Remote URLs are passed to the provider as they are, and the provider downloads them; Inferlo never fetches them. If a provider cannot download a URL, send base64 instead.
- Works with `ai.stream`, `output` and `tools` too. Invalid images raise IL5012 before any model is called.
- In tests, `mockProvider` receives the images on `request.messages[i].images`.

## Structured output

Pass a schema and get typed, validated data back:

```ts
const Triage = t.object({
  priority: t.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]),
  summary: t.string().max(300).describe("One sentence for the agent"),
});

const { object } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: ticket.body, output: Triage });
object.priority; // "low" | "normal" | "urgent"
```

Inferlo sends the JSON Schema to the model, extracts the JSON (tolerating code fences), validates it, and if it does not match, asks the model once to fix it, quoting the exact problems. If it still fails you get IL5002. Model fields can be reused directly: `priority: Ticket.fields.priority`.

## Tools: let the model call your functions

Make a tool from a plain function with `tool(name, { description, input }).handle(fn)` and pass it in `tools`. Function tools work everywhere: with `createAI` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai` in any framework, and with `ctx.ai` in a route handler, next to route tools.

```ts
import { createAI, tool, t, httpError } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai";

export const getWeather = tool("getWeather", {
  description: "Current weather for a city",
  input: t.object({ city: t.string(), unit: t.enum(["c", "f"]).default("c") }),
}).handle(async ({ input, signal }) => {
  const weather = await weatherApi(input.city, input.unit, { signal });
  if (!weather) throw httpError(404, `No weather for ${input.city}.`);
  return weather;
});

const { text, steps } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: "Do I need an umbrella in Oslo?", tools: [getWeather] });
```

- **Input is validated.** The model's arguments are checked against `input` (defaults applied) before your function runs. Invalid arguments go back to the model as a failed tool result with status 422 and IL1001, so it can correct itself.
- **Output** is any JSON value, sent to the model as JSON, or a string, sent as it is. `steps[i].toolCalls` has the `output` with status 200.
- **Errors.** Throw `httpError(404, "...")` (or `notFound`, `forbidden`, any `InferloError` with a status below 500) to send a failed tool result to the model. Any other error is not hidden: `ai.generate` rejects with it, after reporting the usage so far.
- **Names** are letters, digits, `_` and `-` (the provider limit), and must be unique in one call. Invalid definitions raise IL5013.
- `signal` is the `ai.generate` call's `signal`, so long tools stop with the call.
- Step limit, usage per step, budgets and fallback work as for route tools below.

## Tools: let the model call your routes

Pass routes as `tools` and the model can call them while it works out its answer. Each tool call runs as an HTTP request to the route **as the current user**: the route's `auth`, roles and schema validation apply exactly as they do for any other client, so a model can never do more than the user could.

```ts
import { route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { createTicket, getTicket, listTickets } from "./tickets.ts";

export const assistant = route
  .post("/assistant", { body: t.object({ message: t.string().max(4000) }) })
  .handle(async ({ ai, body, user }) => {
    const { text, steps, usage } = await ai.generate({
      model: "smart",
      system: "You help users manage their support tickets.",
      prompt: body.message,
      tools: [createTicket, getTicket, listTickets],
      maxSteps: 5,
      for: user.id,
    });
    return { reply: text, toolCalls: steps.flatMap((s) => s.toolCalls.map((c) => c.name)), cost: usage.cost };
  });
```

- **Names and arguments** come from the route: the tool name is the route's export name (`createTicket`, or `tool: { name }`), the description is `tool.description`, `description` or `summary`, and the arguments are the route's `params`, `query` and `body` fields in one JSON Schema (the same tool the MCP server shows). Routes do not need `tool: true` to be used here; that option only controls the MCP server.
- **Errors go back to the model.** A 403, 404 or 422 from the route (or an unknown tool name) is sent to the model as a failed tool result, so it can correct itself.
- **Step limit.** `maxSteps` (default 5) is the most model calls, tool rounds plus the final answer. A model still calling tools at the limit raises IL5010.
- **Usage per step.** `steps` lists every model call with its `text`, `toolCalls` (`name`, `input`, `status`, `output`, `isError`) and `usage`; `usage` has the totals and is reported to `onUsage` once. `allow` is checked again before every model call that follows tool calls, so budgets stop a long run.
- **Fallback.** Once a tool has run, Inferlo does not retry on the next model in the alias (that would run the tools again); the call fails with IL5006.
- **Structured output** works with tools: pass `output` and the final answer is validated as usual.
- Works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and OpenAI-compatible servers whose models support tool calling. Route tools only work through `ctx.ai` inside a route handler (IL5009), and must be routes registered in `createApp` (IL5011); function tools work anywhere. Streaming with tools is not supported yet.

In tests, a `mockProvider` can return tool calls:

```ts
mockProvider({
  respond: (r) => (r.messages.at(-1)!.role === "tool" ? "Created it." : { toolCalls: [{ name: "createTicket", input: { title: "Printer on fire" } }] }),
});
```

## Streaming

```ts
export const chat = route
  .post("/chat", { body: t.object({ message: t.string().max(4000) }) })
  .handle(({ body, ai, user }) => ai.stream({ model: "fast", prompt: body.message, for: user.id }).toResponse());
```

`toResponse()` sends server-sent events: `text` events with JSON-encoded chunks, then a `done` event with usage. You can also iterate: `for await (const chunk of ai.stream(...))`, or `await stream.text()`.

## Embeddings

```ts
const { embeddings } = await ai.embed({ input: ["first text", "second text"] });   // uses the "embed" alias
cosineSimilarity(embeddings[0], embeddings[1]);
```

## Usage and budgets

Every call reports a `Usage` record (`requested`, `model` that answered, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cost`, `for`, `kind`, `durationMs`) to `onUsage`. Store it to bill customers. When `for` is set, `allow` is called first; returning false raises IL5004 (HTTP 402).

## Testing

```ts
import { mockProvider } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

ai: { providers: { mock: mockProvider({ respond: () => '{"priority":"urgent","summary":"Down"}' }) }, models: { fast: "mock:test" } }
```

---

# Background jobs

Jobs run work after the response is sent, with retries: sending email, calling a slow AI model, processing an upload. A job is a plain value, like a route.

```ts
// src/jobs.ts
import { job, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const summarizeNote = job("summarize-note", {
  input: t.object({ noteId: t.uuid() }),
  retries: 3,              // default 3: up to 4 runs in total
  summary: "Write an AI summary of a note",
}).handle(async ({ input, db, ai, attempt }) => {
  const note = await db.notes.get(input.noteId);
  const { text } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: `Summarize:\n\n${note.body}`, for: note.ownerId });
  await db.notes.update(note.id, { summary: text });
});
```

Register jobs in `createApp`, like routes:

```ts
import * as jobs from "./jobs.ts";

export const app = createApp({ models, routes: [notes], jobs: [jobs], ... });
```

## Enqueue

From a route handler, with `ctx.jobs`:

```ts
export const createNote = route
  .post("/notes", { body: Note.pick("title", "body") })
  .handle(async ({ body, user, db, jobs, status }) => {
    const note = await db.notes.insert({ ...body, ownerId: user.id });
    await jobs.enqueue(summarizeNote, { noteId: note.id });
    status(201);
    return note;
  });
```

Anywhere else, with `app.jobs.enqueue(job, input)`.

- Pass the job itself, not its name, so the input is typed and checked by TypeScript.
- The input is validated against the job's schema when it is enqueued (IL1001 if it does not match) and again when the job runs. It is stored as JSON, so pass ids, not rows: dates arrive as ISO strings and `t.date()` turns them back into `Date`.
- `enqueue(job, input, { runAt: new Date(Date.now() + 60_000) })` runs the job no earlier than `runAt`.
- `enqueue` returns the job record: `{ id, name, input, status, attempts, maxAttempts, runAt, lastError?, createdAt, updatedAt }`. `app.jobs.get(id)` reads it again. `status` is `"pending"`, `"running"`, `"done"` or `"failed"`.

## Handlers

The handler receives `{ input, db, ai, jobs, cache, audit, id, attempt }` (`cache` is the app cache, see [Caching](caching.md)). `attempt` is 1 on the first run. `jobs.enqueue` inside a job queues follow-up jobs. There is no signed-in user: pass the user id in the input and use `for: userId` on AI calls. `ai.generate({ tools })` only works in route handlers (IL5009).

Throw to fail an attempt. A failed job runs again after 10 seconds, then 20, 40, and so on (at most one hour between attempts), until its retries are used up; then its status is `"failed"` and the error is logged. `lastError` holds the last error message. Make handlers safe to run twice: a retry runs the whole handler again.

## Running jobs

```ts
// src/server.ts
const server = await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
app.jobs.start();                      // runs due jobs every second (pollMs: 1000)
process.on("SIGTERM", () => void app.close());   // stops the worker, waits for the running job
```

New projects do this in `src/server.ts`. `app.close()` stops every worker started with `app.jobs.start()` and waits for its running job, together with in-flight requests, then closes the server and the database (see [graceful shutdown](deploy.md#graceful-shutdown)). To stop only the jobs, keep the worker and call `await worker.stop()`.

To run jobs in separate processes, keep them in the database (below) and start `inferlo worker` (`npm run worker` in new projects). It runs `app.jobs.start()` and, on SIGTERM or Ctrl+C, waits for the running job before it exits. Web servers and workers share the queue, so you can run jobs in both or only in workers. See [CLI](cli.md#inferlo-worker).

## Cron

`cron(schedule, job)` queues a job on a schedule. Export it next to the job; registering the module registers both:

```ts
// src/jobs.ts
import { cron, job, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const deleteOldSessions = job("delete-old-sessions", { input: t.object({}) }).handle(async ({ db }) => {
  await db.sessions.deleteMany({ expiresAt: { lt: new Date() } });
});

export const nightly = cron("0 3 * * *", deleteOldSessions);   // every day at 03:00 UTC
```

- The schedule has five fields, `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`, always in UTC: numbers, `*`, ranges (`1-5`), lists (`1,15`), steps (`*/15`, `5/20`) and names (`jan`, `mon`). Sunday is `0` or `7`. When both day fields are set, either one matching is enough, as in standard cron. Invalid schedules raise IL6013 when the module loads.
- `"*/15 * * * *"` every 15 minutes, `"0 * * * *"` every hour, `"30 3 * * 1-5"` at 03:30 on weekdays, `"0 0 1 * *"` on the first of each month.
- The job runs with the input `{}`, so its schema must accept it (IL6013 otherwise). Read what it needs from the database.
- Crons run while a worker runs: `app.jobs.start()` or `inferlo worker`. At each tick the job is queued and then runs like any other job, with its retries. Ticks are only queued after the worker started, and if the worker was paused past several ticks, only the latest one is queued.
- Each tick gets a fixed job id, so with the database queue every instance can run the schedule and the job is still queued once per tick.
- `cron.next(date)` returns the first tick after a date, and `app.jobs.crons` lists the crons. To test the work itself, enqueue the job: `await app.jobs.enqueue(deleteOldSessions, {})`, then `await app.jobs.runDue()`.

## Where jobs are kept

By default the queue is kept in memory in the process that enqueues, so jobs are lost on restart and every instance runs its own. That is right for development and tests.

In production, keep jobs in Postgres:

```ts
export const app = createApp({
  db: postgres({ url: env("DATABASE_URL") }),
  jobs: [jobs],
  jobQueue: { store: "database" },     // default "memory"
});
```

- Jobs are stored in the table `inferlo_jobs`, created on first use (no migration needed). They survive restarts and deploys.
- Every instance shares the queue. Due jobs are claimed with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so each attempt runs on exactly one instance, however many run `app.jobs.start()`.
- An instance only claims jobs it has registered, so during a rolling deploy an old instance never picks up a job that only the new code knows.
- While a job runs, its worker reports every 30 seconds that it is still alive. A job still `"running"` without a report for 5 minutes (its process crashed or was killed) is picked up again as its next attempt, with `lastError` saying the worker stopped. If it has no attempts left, it is marked `"failed"` instead. This is why handlers must be safe to run twice.
- `{ store: "database" }` needs the Postgres adapter (IL6012). Any other store name raises IL6011.
- `app.jobs.get(id)` reads the record from the table, so any instance can check a job's status.

## Testing

`app.jobs.runDue()` runs every due job now, one after another, including follow-ups they enqueue, and returns `{ done, retried, failed }`:

```ts
const res = await app.request("/notes", { method: "POST", json: { title: "Hi", body: "..." }, as: user });
assert.deepEqual(await app.jobs.runDue(), { done: 1, retried: 0, failed: 0 });
```

`runDue({ now })` runs the jobs that are due at that time, to test retries and `runAt` without waiting.

`inferlo describe` lists jobs with their retries and input schema, and crons with their schedule.

---

# Caching

Every app has a cache for results that are slow or expensive to compute, and GET routes can cache their whole responses (see [Caching route responses](#caching-route-responses)): reports, counts, responses from other services, AI answers that do not change often. It is `ctx.cache` in routes and jobs and `app.cache` everywhere else (scripts, tests, server startup), all the same cache.

```ts
import { route } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const ticketStats = route.get("/tickets/stats", { summary: "Ticket counts by status" }).handle(({ db, cache }) =>
  cache.getOrSet("tickets:stats", { ttlMs: 60_000, tags: ["tickets"] }, async () => {
    const all = await db.tickets.findMany({});
    return { open: all.filter((t) => t.status === "open").length, total: all.length };
  }),
);

export const closeTicket = route.post("/tickets/:id/close", { params: IdParams }).handle(async ({ db, cache, params }) => {
  const ticket = await db.tickets.update(params.id, { status: "closed" });
  await cache.invalidate("tickets"); // every entry tagged "tickets" is removed
  return ticket;
});
```

## The API

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `await cache.getOrSet(key, { ttlMs, tags }, compute)` | The cached value, or else the result of `compute()`, stored for `ttlMs`. Concurrent calls for the same key in one process share one `compute()` call. When `compute()` throws, nothing is stored and the error is thrown. |
| `await cache.get(key)` | The cached value, or `undefined` when there is none or it expired. `cache.get<Stats>(key)` types the result. |
| `await cache.set(key, value, { ttlMs, tags })` | Store a value for `ttlMs` milliseconds, replacing any entry with the same key. |
| `await cache.delete(key)` | Remove one entry. |
| `await cache.invalidate("tickets")` or `invalidate(["tickets", "users"])` | Remove every entry stored with any of these tags. |
| `await cache.clear()` | Remove every entry. |
| `cache.store` | `"memory"` or `"database"`. |

Prefer `getOrSet`: it is one call, and it cannot forget to store the result.

- **Every entry has a time to live.** `ttlMs` is required, a whole number of milliseconds from 1 to 365 days. There is no entry that lives forever, so stale data always goes away on its own.
- **Tags invalidate groups of entries.** Tag entries with what they depend on (`"tickets"`, `` `user:${user.id}` ``) and call `invalidate` with that tag after a change. This is how to keep cached data correct when the data changes before the time to live is over.
- **Values are stored as JSON.** Plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and `null`. Dates come back as ISO strings, also from `getOrSet` on the first call, so a hit and a miss return the same thing. `undefined`, functions and `BigInt` cannot be cached (IL6028); cache `null` for "nothing". The memory store keeps JSON too, so changing an object you stored or got never changes the cached entry.
- **Keys** are strings of 1 to 512 characters. Build them from what the value depends on: `` `tickets:stats` ``, `` `user:${user.id}:dashboard` ``. A value that differs per user must have the user in its key, so one user never sees another user's data.

## Stores

```ts
createApp({ cache: { store: "memory" } });   // default
createApp({ cache: { store: "database" }, db: postgres({ url: settings.DATABASE_URL }) });
```

- `"memory"` (default): entries live in the process. Fast and fine for one instance and for tests, but each instance has its own entries, and `invalidate` only reaches the instance that calls it.
